To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the conversion factors of nitrogen to protein for the biomass of the microalgal and the cyanobacterial strains tested were 5.94 for Kjeldahl nitrogen and 4.45 for total nitrogen measured using elemental analysis, and the protein content in dry algal biomass was in the range 30% to over 50% of the dry weight of biomass.

the conversion factors for the protein content of dry microalgal biomass obtained from exponentially-growing cells with a steady-state doubling time of approximately one day are 5.95 (nitrogen-to-protein conversion factor measured by the Kjeldhal method) and 4.4 (total nitrogen-to-protein).

(a) the protein content of dry microalgal biomass can be determined by measuring the nitrogen content of the biomass by elemental analysis or by the Kjeldhal method and multiplying the nitrogen value by the nitrogen-to-protein ratio, which depends on the species of microalgae and the growth phase of the cells, and (b) the nitrogen-to-proteins ratio is higher in biomass from exponentially growing cells than in stationary phase cells.

the production of microalgal proteins as food and feed.
the use of microalgae for production of protein and other products.
the development of new technologies to improve the efficiency of production of microalgae, which can be used as a source of food and as a source of renewable energy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the conversion factor for the Lowry method is 4.44, and that the protein content is in the range 30-55% (w/w).
for the microalgae tested, the protein content of biomass is 4.44% N and 5.95% Kjeldahl N, with the conversion factors being dependent on the growth conditions.

protein is a major component of microalgal dry biomass, but its content varies considerably between species, and the protein content in biomass from a given species varies depending on growth conditions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the protein content of biomass from microalgae and cyanobacteria can be measured by the Lowery method following cell disruption by milling.
the conversion factor of 4.44 is the most appropriate for the estimation of the protein content of biomass from cyanobacteria and microalgae.
the Lowry method is a reliable method for measuring protein in biomass of microalgae and cyanobacteria and can be used for rapid screening of microalgal protein content.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the protein content of algal biomass can be determined with a reasonable degree of confidence using the Lowry assay, provided that the biomass is milled with ceramic beads.
the conversion factor for nitrogen-to-protein is not a universal constant but depends on the biomass type and the growth conditions.

the conversion factors for the estimation of the protein content of biomass from elemental analysis are different from those for Kjeldahl analysis, and that the conversion factors are different for different microalgal and/or cyanobacterial strains.
